paragraphs.text: The enemy of truth saw the Lord, the Savior and life-giving God, being proclaimed, and he was troubled. He saw the Lord's coming on a colt, glorified by us as at the first, and he tried to throw it into confusion with the rumble of rolling chariots, so as to stop the colt in its course. But the colt, with its gentle and quiet-paced feet, stopped the chariot-fighting horses of the warriors. For he knew that the colt had been made ready to defeat the chariot horses. The Savior's coming on a colt did not show any weakness. It showed the meekness of humility, so that he might quench arrogance. And since the enemy knew that things would come about as the prophetic word said, he grew jealous and bore a grudge against the colt. But the colt came so that the Lord might quench the pride of the proud, and bring low the great arrogance of the one who exalts himself in chariots and horses.

The blessed prophet rightly announced this beforehand, and gave encouragement by saying: "Do not fear, daughter of Zion; proclaim it and rejoice, daughter of Jerusalem. For behold, your king comes riding on the colt of an ass, to destroy the chariots from Ephraim and the horses from Jerusalem." Do you see how he weakened and brought down swaggering boastfulness by meekness? Just as he took away sufferings by suffering, bound death by death, and put the power of the adversary to shame by the wood of the holy cross, so too by the colt he broke down the horse-riding haughtiness of the arrogant one.

"Rejoice," says the prophet, "daughter of Zion; exult and proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem." For it is right and fitting for those who worship God not only to hold the divine gifts within themselves, but also to spread the proclamation of his kindness to others. "For behold, your king comes, meek and lowly, and seated on a colt." He rightly put "meek" and "lowly" first. In this way he made clear that poverty was not the reason. Rather, it was the good news of meekness and humility. If someone rides a donkey's foal because he has few goods and no horses, it is not counted to him as virtue and humility, for the necessity of want drives him to it. But if someone rich in chariots and with many horses sits on a donkey's foal out of meekness, he adorns the rank of meekness with humility. The King of hosts was not poor in chariots. The Only-begotten did not lack chariots and horses. The prophet says of him, "The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, and thousands are their drivers." He was not poor in chariots, he who yokes the winds and drives them with wondrous and novel reins. Or do you not know that, as horses serve us as mounts, [?] As David says, "He who walks upon the wings of the winds."

So he came on a colt both to break down arrogance by humility and to announce, as good news, a complete figure of the coming in of the Gentiles. For the colt is reckoned among the unclean animals. Moses set apart as unclean every animal that does not have a cloven hoof and does not chew the cud. The ass neither chews the cud nor has a cloven hoof, so it is reckoned among the unclean animals. Here he was fulfilling beforehand the figures of his dispensation, which seeks out humankind. For he was about to call the holy people of divine lineage [?] his steed. Horses are the mounts of riders, and in the same way the souls of the saints are the steeds of God, to be guided and given instruction. As the prophet says, "If you mount your steeds, your riding is salvation." Paul was just such a steed, unruly [?] and unbridled, and he did not heed the divine laws [?]. He grazed in the pastures of the Law and kicked against the graces of the Gospel. When the Son, the Lord of all, put a bridle on him and sat upon him, he said: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad, and to kick against the sword." And since the colt has run off and left the order of my discourse, let us beseech the Lord of the colt, who is able to hold it, lead it, and keep it within the discourse. For he is the one of whom the prophecy says, "He will bind his colt to the vine."

Jesus, who sits upon the cherubim, sat on a colt. Above, he is awesome because of his divine nature. Below, he is longed for because of his gracious love for mankind. Above, the seraphim worship him with trembling, while on earth we who are flesh proclaim him boldly. For as awesome as his birth is on high, so is the freely sprung Shoot longed for here below [?]. Jesus sat on a colt, and the crowds spread their garments before him. The honor was good, yet the honor paid by those who gave it was in no way worthy of him [?]. For God does not seek gifts from people according to his own worth, but according to what those who honor him are able to give. Indeed, there is nothing that could honor God as he deserves. The whole earth could not do it. All the heavens could not do it, even if they were melted into voices. All the voices of angels and archangels, all the tongues of beings visible and invisible together, are not enough to glorify him as he deserves.

He who sits forever in the heavenly places mounted a colt. The people spread their garments before him, though they ought first to have spread their souls before him, and only then their garments. You who spread your garments for the colt to tread on, spread out your soul as a dwelling for God. This is what John the Baptist preached: "Prepare the way of the Lord, and make straight the trodden paths." That is, make your souls ready, so that God, the Son of the Lord [?], may enter and dwell in them. And they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him. The one whom angels glorify with awe in heaven, the children on earth blessed with rejoicing, saying "Hosanna." In the Hebrew language this word means glorification and great praise.
